blocks.en: Text: 1 Peter 4:12-19
blocks.es_reference: Texto: 1 Pedro 4:12-19 (RVG)

blocks.en: "Beloved, do not think it strange concerning the fiery trial which is to try you, as though some strange thing happened to you; but rejoice to the extent that you partake of Christ's sufferings, that when His glory is revealed, you may also be glad with exceeding joy." — 1 Peter 4:12-13 (NKJV)
blocks.es_reference: "Amados, no os sorprendáis del fuego de prueba que os ha sobrevenido para probaros, como si alguna cosa extraña os aconteciese; antes bien gozaos de que sois participantes de las aflicciones de Cristo; para que también en la revelación de su gloria os gocéis con gran alegría." — 1 Pedro 4:12-13 (RVG)

blocks.en: Do Not Think the Fiery Trial Strange
blocks.es_reference: No Os Sorprendáis del Fuego de Prueba

blocks.en: Peter now returns to the great theme of the whole letter — suffering — and addresses it head-on. He calls his readers beloved, for he is about to speak tenderly to people in pain. "Beloved, do not think it strange concerning the fiery trial which is to try you, as though some strange thing happened to you" (1 Peter 4:12). The first lesson is simply this: do not be surprised. The Christians receiving this letter were tempted to think that their suffering meant something had gone terribly wrong, that perhaps God had forsaken them. Peter corrects that at once. Suffering is not strange for the followers of a crucified Lord; it is the normal road. The word he uses, fiery trial, pictures suffering as a furnace. As we saw earlier in this letter, fire does not come to destroy the believer's faith but to test and refine it, as a refiner's fire purifies gold. The fire is real and hot, but it is not pointless, and it is not a sign of God's absence.
blocks.es_reference: Pedro vuelve ahora al gran tema de toda la carta — el sufrimiento — y lo aborda de frente. Llama a sus lectores amados, pues está por hablar tiernamente a personas que sufren. "Amados, no os sorprendáis del fuego de prueba que os ha sobrevenido para probaros, como si alguna cosa extraña os aconteciese" (1 Pedro 4:12). La primera lección es sencillamente esta: no os sorprendáis. Los cristianos que recibían esta carta eran tentados a pensar que su sufrimiento significaba que algo había salido terriblemente mal, que tal vez Dios los había abandonado. Pedro lo corrige de inmediato. El sufrimiento no es extraño para los seguidores de un Señor crucificado; es el camino normal. La palabra que usa, fuego de prueba, retrata el sufrimiento como un horno. Como vimos antes en esta carta, el fuego no viene a destruir la fe del creyente sino a probarla y refinarla, como el fuego del refinador purifica el oro. El fuego es real y caliente, pero no es inútil, y no es señal de la ausencia de Dios.

blocks.en: Then Peter says something the world can never understand. "But rejoice to the extent that you partake of Christ's sufferings, that when His glory is revealed, you may also be glad with exceeding joy" (1 Peter 4:13). He does not merely tell them to endure; he tells them to rejoice. The reason is that in their suffering they are partaking of Christ's own sufferings, sharing in some small measure what their Lord endured for them. And there is a glory coming: when Christ's glory is revealed at His appearing, those who shared His sufferings will be glad with exceeding joy. So present pain and future joy are bound tightly together. The trial is not strange, not meaningless, and not the end of the story; it is a fellowship with Christ that leads to glory.
blocks.es_reference: Luego Pedro dice algo que el mundo nunca puede entender. "Antes bien gozaos de que sois participantes de las aflicciones de Cristo; para que también en la revelación de su gloria os gocéis con gran alegría" (1 Pedro 4:13). No les dice meramente que soporten; les dice que se gocen. La razón es que en su sufrimiento son participantes de las aflicciones de Cristo, compartiendo en alguna pequeña medida lo que su Señor sufrió por ellos. Y hay una gloria que viene: cuando la gloria de Cristo sea revelada en su aparición, los que compartieron sus aflicciones se gozarán con gran alegría. Así que el dolor presente y el gozo futuro están estrechamente ligados. La prueba no es extraña, ni inútil, ni el fin de la historia; es una comunión con Cristo que lleva a la gloria.

blocks.en: This was hard-won wisdom for the early church. These scattered believers had perhaps expected that coming to Christ would make life easier, and instead they found themselves slandered, shut out, and in some places in danger of their very lives. Peter does not pretend the fire is not real, nor does he tell them to go looking for suffering; the Christian never courts persecution for its own sake. But when the fire comes, as it will, he is not to be thrown into confusion as though God had lost control. The same Lord who walked the road of the cross told His people plainly that the servant is not greater than his Master, and that if the world hated Him, it will hate those who are His. And there is comfort here: a trial expected is a trial already half-borne, for it cannot take the believer by surprise or drive him to despair.
blocks.es_reference: Esta fue sabiduría ganada a duras penas para la iglesia primitiva. Estos creyentes esparcidos quizá habían esperado que venir a Cristo haría la vida más fácil, y en cambio se hallaron calumniados, excluidos, y en algunos lugares en peligro de sus propias vidas. Pedro no finge que el fuego no es real, ni les dice que vayan en busca del sufrimiento; el cristiano nunca corteja la persecución por sí misma. Pero cuando el fuego viene, como vendrá, no ha de ser arrojado a la confusión como si Dios hubiera perdido el control. El mismo Señor que anduvo el camino de la cruz dijo claramente a su pueblo que el siervo no es mayor que su Señor, y que si el mundo le aborreció a Él, aborrecerá a los que son suyos. Y hay consuelo aquí: una prueba esperada es una prueba ya medio sobrellevada, pues no puede tomar al creyente por sorpresa ni arrojarlo a la desesperación.

blocks.en: Blessed When Reproached for the Name
blocks.es_reference: Bienaventurados Cuando Sois Vituperados por el Nombre

blocks.en: "If you are reproached for the name of Christ, blessed are you, for the Spirit of glory and of God rests upon you. On their part He is blasphemed, but on your part He is glorified" (1 Peter 4:14). To be reproached is to be insulted, mocked, and slandered. The believers were being shamed simply because they bore the name of Christ. Peter's response turns the world's verdict upside down: such a one is not disgraced but blessed. The reason is staggering: the Spirit of glory and of God rests upon the one who suffers for Christ's name. The very presence of God attends those who bear reproach for Him, as the cloud of glory once rested upon the tabernacle. And notice the two sides of the same name: on the part of the mockers, the name of Christ is blasphemed; but on the part of the suffering believer, that same name is glorified. What the enemy means as an insult, God receives as glory.
blocks.es_reference: "Si sois vituperados por el nombre de Cristo, sois bienaventurados; porque el Espíritu de gloria y de Dios reposa sobre vosotros. Ciertamente, según ellos, él es blasfemado, mas según vosotros es glorificado" (1 Pedro 4:14). Ser vituperado es ser insultado, burlado y calumniado. Los creyentes eran avergonzados simplemente porque llevaban el nombre de Cristo. La respuesta de Pedro vuelve del revés el veredicto del mundo: tal persona no es deshonrada sino bienaventurada. La razón es asombrosa: el Espíritu de gloria y de Dios reposa sobre el que sufre por el nombre de Cristo. La presencia misma de Dios acompaña a los que llevan vituperio por Él, como la nube de gloria reposaba en otro tiempo sobre el tabernáculo. Y note los dos lados del mismo nombre: de parte de los burladores, el nombre de Cristo es blasfemado; pero de parte del creyente que sufre, ese mismo nombre es glorificado. Lo que el enemigo intenta como insulto, Dios lo recibe como gloria.

blocks.en: Suffer as a Christian, Not as an Evildoer
blocks.es_reference: Padecer como Cristiano, No como Malhechor

blocks.en: Peter now adds a careful and necessary distinction. "But let none of you suffer as a murderer, a thief, an evildoer, or as a busybody in other people's matters. Yet if anyone suffers as a Christian, let him not be ashamed, but let him glorify God in this matter" (1 Peter 4:15-16). Not all suffering is honorable. If a believer suffers because he has committed murder or theft, or done evil, or even because he has been a meddling busybody prying into other people's affairs, that suffering is deserved and brings no honor at all. The believer must make sure that when he suffers, it is never for wrongdoing. But there is another kind of suffering entirely: to suffer as a Christian, simply for belonging to Christ. Of this the believer is never to be ashamed; rather, he is to glorify God in that very name. The word Christian was often flung as an insult in those days, a term of contempt for the followers of Jesus. Peter takes that insult and makes it a badge of honor. To be called a Christian, and to suffer for it, is not shame but glory, a name in which to praise God.
blocks.es_reference: Pedro añade ahora una distinción cuidadosa y necesaria. "Pero ninguno de vosotros padezca como homicida, o ladrón, o malhechor, o por entremeterse en lo ajeno. Pero si alguno padece como cristiano, no se avergüence; antes glorifique a Dios por ello" (1 Pedro 4:15-16). No todo sufrimiento es honroso. Si un creyente sufre porque ha cometido homicidio o robo, o ha hecho el mal, o aun porque ha sido un entremetido husmeando en los asuntos ajenos, ese sufrimiento es merecido y no trae honor alguno. El creyente debe asegurarse de que, cuando sufra, nunca sea por el mal hacer. Pero hay otra clase de sufrimiento enteramente distinta: padecer como cristiano, simplemente por pertenecer a Cristo. De esto el creyente nunca ha de avergonzarse; más bien, ha de glorificar a Dios por ese mismo nombre. La palabra cristiano a menudo se lanzaba como insulto en aquellos días, un término de desprecio para los seguidores de Jesús. Pedro toma ese insulto y lo hace una insignia de honor. Ser llamado cristiano, y sufrir por ello, no es vergüenza sino gloria, un nombre en el cual alabar a Dios.

blocks.en: Judgment Begins at the House of God
blocks.es_reference: El Juicio Comienza por la Casa de Dios

blocks.en: "For the time has come for judgment to begin at the house of God; and if it begins with us first, what will be the end of those who do not obey the gospel of God?" — 1 Peter 4:17 (NKJV)
blocks.es_reference: "Porque es tiempo de que el juicio comience por la casa de Dios; y si primero comienza por nosotros, ¿cuál será el fin de aquellos que no obedecen al evangelio de Dios?" — 1 Pedro 4:17 (RVG)

blocks.en: Peter now sets the believers' suffering in a larger and more solemn frame. "For the time has come for judgment to begin at the house of God; and if it begins with us first, what will be the end of those who do not obey the gospel of God? Now 'If the righteous one is scarcely saved, where will the ungodly and the sinner appear?'" (1 Peter 4:17-18). There is a sense in which the very trials of God's people are the beginning of God's judging, refining work, and it begins not with the world but with His own household. God purifies His people first, putting them through the fire to make them holy. This is not His rejection of them but His fatherly purifying of them. Yet Peter reasons from this to a sobering warning. If judgment begins with God's own children, and if even the righteous are saved only as through fire, scarcely and with difficulty, then what will become of those who do not obey the gospel? Where will the ungodly and the sinner finally appear? The suffering of the saints is severe, but it ends in salvation and glory; the end of the disobedient is far more fearful. The thought both steadies the believer and warns the lost.
blocks.es_reference: Pedro pone ahora el sufrimiento de los creyentes en un marco mayor y más solemne. "Porque es tiempo de que el juicio comience por la casa de Dios; y si primero comienza por nosotros, ¿cuál será el fin de aquellos que no obedecen al evangelio de Dios? Y si el justo con dificultad se salva, ¿en dónde aparecerá el impío y el pecador?" (1 Pedro 4:17-18). Hay un sentido en que las pruebas mismas del pueblo de Dios son el comienzo de la obra de Dios de juzgar y refinar, y comienza no por el mundo sino por su propia casa. Dios purifica primero a su pueblo, pasándolo por el fuego para hacerlo santo. Esto no es su rechazo de ellos sino su purificación paternal de ellos. Pero Pedro razona de esto a una advertencia solemne. Si el juicio comienza por los propios hijos de Dios, y si aun el justo se salva solo como por fuego, con dificultad y a duras penas, entonces ¿qué será de los que no obedecen al evangelio? ¿En dónde aparecerán finalmente el impío y el pecador? El sufrimiento de los santos es severo, pero termina en salvación y gloria; el fin de los desobedientes es mucho más temible. El pensamiento a la vez afirma al creyente y advierte al perdido.

blocks.en: Commit Your Soul to a Faithful Creator
blocks.es_reference: Encomendad Vuestra Alma a un Fiel Creador

blocks.en: Having said all this, Peter draws it together into one grand command. "Therefore let those who suffer according to the will of God commit their souls to Him in doing good, as to a faithful Creator" (1 Peter 4:19). Here is the whole response of the believer to suffering, gathered into a single sentence. Those who suffer according to the will of God — for it is sometimes God's will that His people suffer — are to do two things. First, they are to commit their souls to God, handing themselves over entirely to His safekeeping rather than trusting to their own defense or seeking their own revenge. The word pictures a deposit placed in trusted hands. Second, they are to keep doing good, continuing to live rightly and lovingly even in the middle of their pain, never letting suffering turn them bitter or sinful. And the ground of this whole trust is the character of the One they trust: He is a faithful Creator. The God who made them will not fail them or forsake them; He keeps what is committed to Him. So the suffering believer places his very soul into the hands of a Creator who is utterly faithful, and goes on quietly doing good, certain that he is safe.
blocks.es_reference: Habiendo dicho todo esto, Pedro lo reúne en un gran mandamiento. "Por tanto, los que padecen según la voluntad de Dios, encomienden sus almas a él, como a fiel Creador, haciendo el bien" (1 Pedro 4:19). He aquí toda la respuesta del creyente al sufrimiento, reunida en una sola oración. Los que padecen según la voluntad de Dios — pues a veces es la voluntad de Dios que su pueblo sufra — han de hacer dos cosas. Primero, han de encomendar sus almas a Dios, entregándose enteramente a su resguardo en vez de confiar en su propia defensa o buscar su propia venganza. La palabra retrata un depósito puesto en manos de confianza. Segundo, han de seguir haciendo el bien, continuando en vivir recta y amorosamente aun en medio de su dolor, sin dejar jamás que el sufrimiento los vuelva amargos o pecadores. Y el fundamento de toda esta confianza es el carácter de Aquel en quien confían: Él es un fiel Creador. El Dios que los hizo no les fallará ni los abandonará; guarda lo que se le encomienda. Así que el creyente que sufre pone su alma misma en las manos de un Creador que es absolutamente fiel, y sigue calladamente haciendo el bien, seguro de que está a salvo.

blocks.en: It is fitting that this great section on suffering ends with the word Creator. The God who is able to keep the believer’s soul is the very One who made him, and nothing in all creation is beyond the reach or the care of the One who made it. The believer entrusts himself, then, not to fate, not to luck, not even merely to a kind friend, but to the almighty and faithful Maker of heaven and earth, who has never once failed a soul that was placed in His hands. Here is the quiet confidence that has carried God’s people through the fire in every century: come what may, the soul committed to a faithful Creator is utterly safe, and the believer is set free to go on doing good without fear.
blocks.es_reference: Es apropiado que esta gran sección sobre el sufrimiento termine con la palabra Creador. El Dios que es capaz de guardar el alma del creyente es el mismo que lo hizo, y nada en toda la creación está fuera del alcance o del cuidado de Aquel que la hizo. El creyente se encomienda, pues, no a la suerte, no al azar, ni siquiera meramente a un amigo bondadoso, sino al todopoderoso y fiel Hacedor del cielo y de la tierra, que jamás ha fallado ni una sola vez a un alma que fue puesta en sus manos. He aquí la callada confianza que ha llevado al pueblo de Dios por el fuego en cada siglo: pase lo que pase, el alma encomendada a un fiel Creador está absolutamente segura, y el creyente queda libre para seguir haciendo el bien sin temor.

blocks.en: "...let those who suffer according to the will of God commit their souls to Him in doing good, as to a faithful Creator." — 1 Peter 4:19 (NKJV)
blocks.es_reference: "...los que padecen según la voluntad de Dios, encomienden sus almas a él, como a fiel Creador, haciendo el bien." — 1 Pedro 4:19 (RVG)

sa.prompt: Explain verses 12-13 — why the believer should not be surprised by the fiery trial, and how he can rejoice.

Then, far beyond mere endurance, Peter tells them to rejoice, because in their suffering they partake of Christ's own sufferings, sharing in some measure what their Lord endured. And present sharing in His sufferings leads to exceeding joy when His glory is revealed at His appearing. So the trial is neither strange nor meaningless; it is a fellowship with Christ that ends in glory, and that is why the believer can rejoice even in the fire.

So what the enemy means as an insult, God receives as glory, and the reproach itself becomes a blessing and a mark that God's own Spirit rests upon His servant.

sa.prompt: Explain verse 19 — committing the soul to a faithful Creator while doing good.
sa.model: Peter draws everything together into one grand command. Those who suffer according to the will of God, for it is sometimes His will that His people suffer, are to do two things. First, they are to commit their souls to God, handing themselves over entirely to His safekeeping rather than trusting in their own defense or seeking their own revenge; the word pictures a deposit placed into trusted hands. Second, they are to keep doing good, continuing to live rightly and lovingly even in the middle of their pain, never letting suffering turn them bitter or sinful. The ground of this whole trust is the character of the One they trust, for He is a faithful Creator: the God who made them will not fail or forsake them but keeps what is committed to Him. So the sufferer rests his soul in faithful hands and goes on doing good.

sa.prompt: Why does the lesson say suffering for Christ is not strange but normal for the Christian?
sa.model: The lesson teaches that the fiery trial is not strange or abnormal but the normal experience of those who follow a crucified Lord. Peter expressly says not to be surprised, as though some strange thing were happening. Because Christ Himself suffered, His followers should expect to share in suffering, for it is part of belonging to Him and not evidence that something has gone wrong. To be surprised by suffering is to misunderstand the Christian life altogether. Rather, the believer should expect trial, recognize it as a real sharing in Christ's own sufferings, and even rejoice in it. The path of suffering is the road the Lord Himself walked, and it is the road that leads to glory, so the Christian meets it not with shock or dismay but as a normal and expected part of faithfully following Christ.

sa.prompt: Explain the honor Peter attaches to the name 'Christian' in this passage.
sa.model: In Peter's day the name Christian was often spoken as an insult, a term of reproach thrown at the followers of Christ. But Peter turns it into a badge of honor. He says that if anyone suffers as a Christian, he should not be ashamed but should glorify God in that very name. To bear the name of Christ, even under reproach, is to be blessed, for the Spirit of glory rests upon such a one. So the very name meant to shame the believer becomes a name of honor and glory. The Christian wears it proudly, not because the world esteems it, but because it identifies him with Christ and brings glory to God. What men intended as contempt, Peter teaches the believer to receive as a title of highest honor, a name worth suffering for and a name in which to praise God.

sa.prompt: How does this passage connect the believer's present suffering with future glory?
sa.model: The passage binds present suffering tightly to future glory. Peter tells believers to rejoice now to the extent that they partake of Christ's sufferings, precisely so that when His glory is revealed they may be glad with exceeding joy. The present pain and the future joy are linked, for those who share Christ's sufferings now will share His glory then. Already the Spirit of glory rests upon them in their reproach, a foretaste of the glory that is coming. So suffering is not the opposite of glory but the very path to it. The believer endures, and even rejoices, in the trial because he knows it leads to the revealing of Christ's glory and to overflowing joy in that day. The fire of today is the seed of the joy of tomorrow, and the road of suffering runs straight to glory.

sa.prompt: How does verse 19 sum up the believer's whole response to suffering?
sa.model: Verse 19 gathers the believer's whole response to suffering into a single sentence. Those who suffer according to the will of God are to do two things. First, they commit their souls to God, entrusting themselves wholly to His keeping rather than to their own defense or revenge. Second, they keep doing good, continuing in obedience and love even under affliction, refusing to let pain make them bitter or turn them to sin. And the ground of it all is that God is a faithful Creator, who made them and will not fail them. So the believer's response to suffering is neither despair nor retaliation but trust and faithfulness: he places his very soul into the hands of a faithful God and goes on doing right, certain that the Creator will keep what is committed to Him. In trust and well-doing the whole answer to suffering is summed up.

sa.prompt: Summarize the central message of Unit 11 (1 Peter 4:12-19).
sa.model: Unit 11 brings the letter's theme of suffering to full voice. Peter tells the beloved not to think the fiery trial strange, for suffering is the normal path of those who follow Christ; rather they should rejoice to partake of Christ's sufferings, that they may have exceeding joy when His glory is revealed. Those reproached for the name of Christ are blessed, for the Spirit of glory rests on them. None should suffer as a murderer or evildoer, but whoever suffers as a Christian should not be ashamed but glorify God in that name, which is a badge of honor. Judgment begins at the house of God, who refines His own first; and if the righteous are scarcely saved, the fate of the ungodly is far more fearful. Therefore those who suffer according to God's will are to commit their souls to a faithful Creator while continuing to do good.
